accepted.s: Which pair of planets is known to rotate in the direction opposite to the usual west-to-east rotation of most planets?
o: Venus and Uranus
Mars and Uranus
Jupiter and Neptune
Mercury and Venus
accepted.x: Venus and Uranus rotate in the opposite direction to the usual west-to-east rotation. Aryabhata was among the earliest scholars to propose that the Earth rotates on its axis.
accepted.tq: Use the confusable-pair method to distinguish the two exceptional planets from the general rule.
accepted.sec: Rotation - direction, period, speed with latitude, circle of illumination, why not felt  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The Earth completes one rotation with respect to the background stars in approximately:
o: 23 hours 30 minutes
23 hours 56 minutes 4 seconds
24 hours 4 minutes
25 hours 6 minutes
accepted.x: A sidereal rotation of the Earth takes approximately 23 hours, 56 minutes and 4 seconds.
accepted.tq: Identify the precise numerical value rather than confusing rotation with the 24-hour solar day.
accepted.sec: Rotation - direction, period, speed with latitude, circle of illumination, why not felt  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the speed of Earth's rotation:
1. It is approximately 1,670 km per hour at the Equator.
2. It decreases with increase in latitude.
3. It becomes zero at the poles.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
accepted.x: All three statements are correct. Rotational speed is greatest at the Equator, decreases towards the poles and becomes zero at the poles.
accepted.tq: Track the geographical trend from the Equator to the poles and verify the endpoint.
accepted.sec: Rotation - direction, period, speed with latitude, circle of illumination, why not felt  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The circle of illumination passes through both the poles when the Earth is experiencing:
o: An equinox
Perihelion
A solstice
Aphelion
accepted.x: The circle of illumination passes through both poles at the equinoxes, when day and night are broadly equal across the Earth.
accepted.tq: Distinguish equinoxes from solstices by using the position of the circle of illumination.
accepted.sec: Rotation - direction, period, speed with latitude, circle of illumination, why not felt  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Why is the rotation of the Earth generally not felt by persons on its surface?
o: The gravitational force of the Sun cancels Earth's rotation.
The Earth rotates only at night.
The Earth's rotation is confined to the polar regions.
The atmosphere and objects on Earth rotate along with it at a nearly uniform speed.
accepted.x: The motion is nearly uniform, without a perceptible change in velocity, and the atmosphere and objects on Earth move along with the Earth.
accepted.tq: Apply the principle of uniform motion and the co-rotation of the atmosphere.
accepted.sec: Rotation - direction, period, speed with latitude, circle of illumination, why not felt  [APPSC]

accepted.s: A particular coastal location passes successively through two tidal bulges during one day. Which of the following is the most likely result?
o: Four high tides and no low tide
One high tide and one low tide every 24 hours
Tides occurring only during the full moon
Two high tides and two low tides, about 12 hours 25 minutes apart
accepted.x: As the Earth rotates, a place generally passes through two tidal bulges, producing two high tides and two low tides, with successive similar tides about 12 hours 25 minutes apart.
accepted.tq: Follow the movement of a place through the two tidal bulges instead of focusing only on the Moon’s phase.
accepted.sec: Rotation - direction, period, speed with latitude, circle of illumination, why not felt  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly describes spring and neap tides?
o: Spring tides occur only at aphelion, while neap tides occur only at perihelion.
Spring tides occur when the Sun and Moon are at right angles, while neap tides occur at conjunction.
Spring tides occur at new and full Moon, while neap tides occur when the Sun and Moon are approximately at right angles.
Both spring and neap tides occur only once a year.
accepted.x: Spring tides occur when the Sun, Earth and Moon are aligned at new and full Moon. Neap tides occur when the Sun and Moon are at approximately right angles, about seven days later, and each occurs twice a month.
accepted.tq: Discriminate between the alignment conditions and timing of spring and neap tides.
accepted.sec: Rotation - direction, period, speed with latitude, circle of illumination, why not felt  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements about the recent change in the Earth's rotation:
1. Climate-driven melting of ice shifts mass towards the Equator.
2. This raises the Earth's moment of inertia.
3. The change tends to slow the rotation and lengthen the day by about 1.33 milliseconds per century.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
accepted.x: All three statements are correct. Redistribution of mass towards the Equator increases moment of inertia and slightly slows Earth's rotation, lengthening the day by about 1.33 milliseconds per century.
accepted.tq: Trace the cause-effect chain from mass redistribution to moment of inertia and rotational slowing.
accepted.sec: Rotation - direction, period, speed with latitude, circle of illumination, why not felt  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The Coriolis force is fundamentally caused by:
o: The gravitational attraction of the Moon alone
The revolution of the Earth around the Sun
The rotation of the Earth on its axis
The unequal heating of land and water
accepted.x: The Coriolis force is an apparent force arising from the rotation of the Earth and affects moving air and water.
accepted.tq: Use the cause-based identification method for a named geographical force.
accepted.sec: Coriolis force - deflection, variation with latitude and wind speed, Ferrel's law  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which of the following correctly states Ferrel's law?
o: Moving air is deflected towards the poles in both hemispheres.
Moving air is deflected towards the Equator in both hemispheres.
Moving air is deflected to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.
Moving air is deflected to the left in the Northern Hemisphere and to the right in the Southern Hemisphere.
accepted.x: Ferrel's law states that the Coriolis effect deflects moving air and water to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.
accepted.tq: Remember the hemispheric reversal by pairing right-Northern with left-Southern.
accepted.sec: Coriolis force - deflection, variation with latitude and wind speed, Ferrel's law  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Cyclones rarely form within about 5° of the Equator primarily because:
o: Trade winds do not exist near the Equator.
The sea surface temperature is always low there.
The pressure gradient force is absent there.
The Coriolis force is too weak near the Equator to provide the required rotation.
accepted.x: The Coriolis force is very weak near the Equator, so it generally cannot provide sufficient rotational deflection for cyclone formation within about 5° latitude.
accepted.tq: Apply the latitude dependence of the Coriolis force to cyclone formation.
accepted.sec: Coriolis force - deflection, variation with latitude and wind speed, Ferrel's law  [APPSC]

accepted.s: In the Northern Hemisphere, tropical cyclones generally rotate:
o: In a direction determined only by ocean salinity
From east to west without rotation
Anticlockwise
Clockwise
accepted.x: The Coriolis effect causes tropical cyclones in the Northern Hemisphere to rotate anticlockwise.
accepted.tq: Apply the hemisphere-based deflection rule to the circulation of cyclones.
accepted.sec: Coriolis force - deflection, variation with latitude and wind speed, Ferrel's law  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Earth's orbit is correct?
o: The orbit is parabolic and the Sun lies outside it.
The orbit is perfectly circular and the Earth remains at a constant distance from the Sun.
The orbit is slightly elliptical and the Sun lies at one focus.
The orbit is highly elliptical and the Sun lies at its centre.
accepted.x: The Earth's orbit is slightly elliptical, with the Sun located at one of the two foci of the ellipse.
accepted.tq: Use precise orbital terminology to reject the circular-orbit and central-Sun traps.
accepted.sec: Revolution - orbit shape, perihelion, aphelion, speed, period  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The Earth is nearest to the Sun at approximately:
o: 21 March, at about 150 million km
3 January, at about 147 million km
4 July, at about 147 million km
3 January, at about 152 million km
accepted.x: The Earth reaches perihelion, its nearest point to the Sun, around 3 January, at a distance of approximately 147 million kilometres.
accepted.tq: Match the date, distance and term together to avoid swapping perihelion with aphelion.
accepted.sec: Revolution - orbit shape, perihelion, aphelion, speed, period  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The Earth's farthest position from the Sun, called aphelion, occurs approximately on:
o: 3 January, at about 147 million km
23 September, at about 147 million km
4 July, at about 152 million km
21 June, at about 150 million km
accepted.x: Aphelion occurs around 4 July, when the Earth is approximately 152 million kilometres from the Sun.
accepted.tq: Use the nearest-farthest and January-July contrasts to identify the correct pair.
accepted.sec: Revolution - orbit shape, perihelion, aphelion, speed, period  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The principal centripetal force that keeps the Earth in its orbit around the Sun is provided by:
o: The pressure of solar radiation
The gravitational force of the Sun
The magnetic force of the Sun
The gravitational force of the Moon
accepted.x: The Sun's gravitational attraction acts as the centripetal force that keeps the Earth revolving around it.
accepted.tq: Identify the body supplying the centripetal force rather than the body in motion.
accepted.sec: Revolution - orbit shape, perihelion, aphelion, speed, period  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which of the following is a consequence of the slightly varying Earth-Sun distance during revolution?
o: It makes the Earth's axis lose its inclination every year.
It slightly alters tidal ranges.
It stops the rotation of the Earth at aphelion.
It completely causes the seasons on Earth.
accepted.x: The changing Earth-Sun distance between perihelion and aphelion slightly affects tidal ranges. It is not the principal cause of the seasons.
accepted.tq: Reject the extreme causal claim and identify the limited effect of perihelion and aphelion.
accepted.sec: Revolution - orbit shape, perihelion, aphelion, speed, period  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which one of the following statements about the variation in day length is NOT correct?
o: Variation in day length generally increases with latitude.
All places on Earth experience equal day and night throughout the year.
The Equator experiences approximately 12 hours of day throughout the year.
Beyond the Arctic and Antarctic Circles, the Sun may remain above the horizon for 24 hours in summer.
accepted.x: The statement that all places experience equal day and night throughout the year is incorrect. Equal day and night throughout the year is characteristic of the Equator, while seasonal variation increases with latitude.
accepted.tq: Find the universal statement that wrongly extends an equatorial condition to all latitudes.
accepted.sec: Day and night - causes, day-length variation, midnight sun

accepted.s: The phenomenon in which the Sun remains above the horizon for 24 hours during summer beyond the Arctic or Antarctic Circle is known as:
o: Twilight arc
Midnight sun
Solar eclipse
Polar night
accepted.x: The midnight sun refers to continuous daylight for 24 hours or more in high-latitude regions during their summer.
accepted.tq: Match the distinctive high-latitude phenomenon with its exact term.
accepted.sec: Day and night - causes, day-length variation, midnight sun

accepted.s: Which of the following statements correctly describes the day-night cycle at the poles?
o: The poles experience approximately six months of daylight and six months of darkness.
The poles have the same day length as the Equator throughout the year.
The poles experience exactly 12 hours of day and 12 hours of night every day.
The poles remain permanently in darkness.
accepted.x: Because of the Earth's axial inclination and revolution, the poles experience approximately six months of daylight followed by approximately six months of night.
accepted.tq: Use the extreme-latitude case to distinguish polar conditions from equatorial conditions.
accepted.sec: Day and night - causes, day-length variation, midnight sun

accepted.s: Which statement best distinguishes a sidereal day from a solar day?
o: There is no difference between a sidereal day and a solar day.
A solar day is measured relative to a star and is shorter than a sidereal day.
A sidereal day is measured relative to a star and is about four minutes shorter than a solar day.
A sidereal day is measured from one noon to the next and lasts 23 hours 56 minutes.
accepted.x: A sidereal day, measured relative to a distant star, lasts 23 hours 56 minutes 4 seconds. A solar day, measured from one noon to the next, lasts 24 hours because Earth also moves along its orbit.
accepted.tq: Discriminate the reference point first, then compare the durations.
accepted.sec: Sidereal vs solar day, leap year

accepted.s: The extra approximately one-quarter day accumulated each year is accommodated in the calendar by:
o: Subtracting one day from every leap year
Adding 29 February every four years, subject to the century-year rule
Adding one month at the end of every year
Adding one day every two years
accepted.x: The accumulated extra quarter day produces a leap year with 29 February approximately every four years, with exceptions for century years.
accepted.tq: Connect the fractional annual remainder with the calendar correction.
accepted.sec: Sidereal vs solar day, leap year

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly applies the Gregorian leap-year rule?
o: 1900 was not a leap year, whereas 2000 was a leap year.
1900 was a leap year, whereas 2000 was not a leap year.
Both 1900 and 2000 were leap years because both are divisible by 100.
Neither 1900 nor 2000 was a leap year because century years are excluded.
accepted.x: A century year is a leap year only when divisible by 400. Thus 1900 was not a leap year, while 2000 was a leap year.
accepted.tq: Apply the exception rule after checking divisibility by 400.
accepted.sec: Sidereal vs solar day, leap year

accepted.s: The Foucault pendulum experiment conducted in Paris in 1851 demonstrated the Earth's rotation through:
o: A permanent change in the length of the pendulum
The direct measurement of the Earth's orbital speed
The slow turning of the plane of the pendulum's swing
The rise and fall of ocean tides
accepted.x: In Foucault's 1851 experiment at Paris, the plane of swing of the pendulum slowly turned, providing visible evidence of Earth's rotation.
accepted.tq: Match the experiment with its distinctive observable result and date.
accepted.sec: Evidences and experiments of rotation (Foucault pendulum)

accepted.s: Which of the following is NOT an evidence of the rotation of the Earth?
o: The equatorial bulge
Coriolis deflection of winds and ocean currents
The apparent east-to-west motion of stars and the Sun
The constant distance between the Earth and the Sun throughout the year
accepted.x: The constant Earth-Sun distance is not an evidence of Earth's rotation; in fact, the distance varies slightly because Earth's orbit is elliptical. Coriolis deflection, equatorial bulge and apparent celestial motion are evidences of rotation.
accepted.tq: Identify the unrelated orbital-distance statement among recognised rotation evidences.
accepted.sec: Evidences and experiments of rotation (Foucault pendulum)

accepted.s: Twilight is best defined as:
o: The period when the Sun is directly overhead
The permanent daylight experienced at the poles
Diffused light before sunrise and after sunset
The period of total darkness before sunrise
accepted.x: Twilight is the period of diffused light before sunrise and after sunset, when the Sun is below or near the horizon.
accepted.tq: Use the precise definition to distinguish twilight from daylight and darkness.
accepted.sec: Twilight duration variation with latitude

accepted.s: How does the duration of twilight generally vary with latitude?
o: It occurs only between the Tropics.
It is approximately the same at every latitude.
It is longest at the Equator and shortest at the poles.
It is shortest at the Equator and becomes longer towards the poles.
accepted.x: Twilight is shortest at the Equator because the Sun rises and sets nearly vertically. It lasts longer at high latitudes because the Sun follows an oblique path, becoming weeks-long near the poles.
accepted.tq: Compare the angle of the Sun's path at low and high latitudes.
accepted.sec: Twilight duration variation with latitude

accepted.s: A cyclone approaching the Andhra Pradesh coast is steered towards the north-northwest under the combined influence of steering winds, trade winds and the Coriolis effect. Which statement follows from this description?
o: The Coriolis effect is absent over the Bay of Bengal.
The cyclone's track is determined solely by ocean tides.
The cyclone cannot be affected by winds outside its eye.
Large-scale atmospheric circulation and Earth's rotation can influence the cyclone's path.
accepted.x: Cyclone movement is influenced by steering winds and broader atmospheric circulation, while the Coriolis effect influences its deflection and rotation. These factors are relevant to cyclones striking the Andhra Pradesh coast.
accepted.tq: Apply the roles of steering winds, trade winds and Coriolis deflection to a regional cyclone scenario.
accepted.sec: Universal angles
